picks.title: Sightlines Issue No. 2: what it takes to design agentic products
picks.excerpt: Figma's Sightlines newsletter no.2 gathers senior design and product leaders on what it takes to design agentic products. The core problem: agents are powerful, but interfaces must earn trust and make permissions and security legible to users.
picks.rationale: Senior product leaders on the exact problem designers now face daily — making an agent's permissions and reach legible enough to trust.

picks.title: AI dev tool power rankings: Claude Opus 5 debuts at No. 1, Kimi K3 is the first open-weight model in the top three
picks.excerpt: August's AI dev tool rankings mark the largest single-month shake-up yet: Claude Opus 5 debuts at the top with a 1691 Elo, and Kimi K3 becomes the first open-weight model in the top three. Four new entrants reset which model teams should default to for build work.
picks.rationale: The biggest monthly reshuffle yet in build-tool rankings — it changes which model a design-engineering team should reach for tomorrow.

picks.title: How Dark and Darker's devs used Aura to build a major feature in half the time
picks.excerpt: IRONMACE's non-technical president used the AI coding assistant Aura to build Dark and Darker's tutorial system directly against the game codebase in about two weeks — work the team estimated at five to six weeks. A concrete case of a non-engineer shipping production features.
picks.rationale: A shipped, named example of a non-engineer building a real production feature against a live codebase — the clearest proof yet of where the build boundary moved.

picks.title: How to automate your design system documentation without losing the parts that matter
picks.excerpt: A practical breakdown of which design system documentation should be generated automatically from code and tokens, and which parts — intent, rationale, usage judgement — must stay human-authored. Automating the wrong layer produces docs nobody trusts.
picks.rationale: Draws the line between the docs a generator should own and the rationale a human must write — directly actionable for anyone maintaining a system.

picks.title: AI features users don't want — and what they actually need
picks.excerpt: Most shipped AI features are bolt-on chat panels that add steps instead of removing them. The argument: good AI design is invisible — it absorbs tedious work inside existing flows rather than announcing itself as a new surface.
picks.rationale: A usable test for the next AI feature spec: does it remove a step inside the existing flow, or just add another panel to ignore?
